speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will know that military action began in the Persian Gulf today, as announced at 7 p.m. Eastern Standard Time.
President Bush called me beforehand to apprise me that he had authorized such action. We understand at the moment that the participants of this first wave included forces from the United States, the United Kingdom, Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait.
The fighting is a direct consequence of Saddam Hussein's determination to maintain his brutal occupation and his illegal annexation of Kuwait in defiance of world opinion. He has chosen to ignore the numerous opportunities that were open to him to withdraw. He has had 167 days since his illegal and brutal invasion of Kuwait on August 2, and 48 full days since the United Nations Security Council passed resolution 678 on November 29.
In all of that time, with all of the requests, with all of the appeals from leaders around the world, his answer has been no. Resolution 678 provided a pause for peace and gave Saddam Hussein one final opportunity to comply with the will of the world community, as duly expressed through the United Nations. He refused again and again to take that opportunity. Diplomacy has been given every chance to end this conflict peacefully, but regrettably has failed in the face of Saddam Hussein's intransigence. That same intransigence and his indifference to the suffering of his own people, especially the children, made it clear that sanctions alone were not going to force him to leave Kuwait.
There has not been a single iota of interest on his part in complying with the United Nations directives. The time has regrettably come therefore to act in the
interests of preserving world order and in safeguarding the effectiveness of the United Nations. A failure by the world community to act would have undermined the United Nations, turned a blind eye to naked aggression, condoned violations of international law and encouraged other potential aggressors to defy world opinion in the pursuit of their own criminal ambitions. If Canada had stood aside, we would have betrayed our own national interests, repudiated our own responsibilities and dishonoured our own traditions.
Canada did not stand aside in two world wars and Korea. Canada, and in particular the Secretary of State for External Affairs, did not stand aside from the hard work of seeking a peaceful end to the Iraqi occupation of Kuwait and, Mr. Speaker, Canada is not standing aside tonight from giving effect to the United Nations resolutions.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
We have joined with other UN members in expelling Saddam Hussein from Kuwait by force. At this moment our CF-18s are flying combat air patrol in the northern Persian Gulf, protecting Canadian and allied ships and personnel in the gulf and the Arabian Peninsula. Canadian ships are now engaged in the company of others, in playing a vital role in assuring the support of the seaborn arm of the coalition in the Persian Gulf.
Earlier this evening, the cabinet met and gave the Chief of the Defence Staff, General de Chastelain, authority for the Canadian forces to carry out sweep and escort missions over Kuwait and Iraq, if necessary and appropriate. All Canadian forces in the gulf will nevertheless remain under Canadian command.
I profoundly regret, as I am sure, do all members of this House, that it has come to this. It is with no satisfaction that we take up arms, because war is always a tragedy, but the greater tragedy would have been for criminal aggression to go unchecked.
I am sure that the safety of the Canadian service men and women in the gulf is uppermost in the minds of all members. Our hearts go out tonight to those families with loved ones, fathers or mothers, sons and daughters, and brothers and sisters, on duty in the Persian Gulf. These courageous men and women are braving great danger in the defence of the values and the interests of their entire country. They have our gratitude and our respect, and especially tonight, our prayers.

Now is the time for all Canadians to put aside their differences and rally to their support. I am sure that all hon. members join me and all Canadians in praying that this war will end quickly and that all Canadians will welcome home our brave fellow citizens who defend freedom and the cause of peace.
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise in the House of Commons tonight, my heart is filled with a deep sense of foreboding. Like every Canadian, like the mothers and fathers of those men and women representing us in the Persian Gulf, I am worried. I had hoped that it would not come to this.

This evening, Canada is at war. Operation Desert Storm has begun. This evening, Canada is anxiously following the course of events in the Middle East. Canadian men and women are watching their TV sets, hoping the missiles will spare their families and friends.

While I am Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the Liberal Party, I am also a father and a grandfather and, like the millions of Canadians now sitting clustered around their televisions and radios, I am trying to come to terms with all of this. Tonight, diplomacy and negotiations have given way to bullets and bombs and I am sad about that. But, as the Prime Minister said, I hope that this will be reversed very quickly. As all Canadians who have followed this crisis know, the Liberal Party has urged the government not to go to war. We urged the government to allow more time for the sanctions to work before putting the lives of thousands of Canadian troops at risk.

Unfortunately, diplomacy and negotiations have given way to armed intervention, and I regret this deeply. The Liberal Party has always been opposed to war. No one likes war and no one likes to go to war. All we can hope now is that Iraq will withdraw its troops from Kuwait and that there will be as few victims as possible. The war must not be allowed to go on forever.
Government Orders
On behalf of the families and relatives of our Canadian soldiers, those men and women who perform their duties so bravely and valiantly, we can only hope that this war will be a short one. The price of war is always far too high.

We regret that our request that a search be made for a peaceful solution has fallen on deaf ears but, at the same time, we will support the efforts of our men and women in the Persian Gulf. We are at war, but all of us have to make sure that we are not losing the Canadian ambition, our historic quest for peace. We hope that this war will be short. We hope that all efforts will be made to find avenues to have a cease-fire quickly, in order to make sure that not many men and women lose their lives in that process. We hope that this operation will be successful; we do not think it was necessary. Let us all hope and pray together that it will be short and that those valiant Canadians who are there will be able to come back to their families, as the Prime Minister has said, in good health.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I want to ask the Prime Minister and his cabinet to do everything in their power to restore peace in the Middle East as soon as possible. As we have said before, it is sometimes much more difficult to end a war than to start it. We hope that we will have peace again very soon, because we sincerely believed a few months ago that a new international order had been established.
The cold war being over, we felt that it would be possible to find peaceful solutions to world problems and now we find to our dismay that a real war can start so quickly.
We are all Canadians and we must support our brothers and sisters fighting for peace. I rise tonight to say that all Canadians have the obligation to stand united under such circumstances.

As Canadians, we have differences. I said that it was not the right way, but we are at war and we have to be united because Canadians are fighting right now. I hope that none go down in fighting. We have to back them up.

January 16, 1991
Government Orders
It is a different way than the way we would have chosen, but they are fighting for peace. We hope that they will be very successful in a very short order.

Mr. Speaker, our first thought tonight, like all Canadians I am sure, is for the men and women who are in the Middle East and the families of those men and women.
It is surely, whatever one's opinion is, a great tragedy for Canada and for those people. It does not in any way undermine the fact that they are there, that war has become a reality and that our thoughts and prayers are with them.
[ Translation]
My party and I are proud of the contribution made by Canadian men and women in the Middle East to enforce the sanctions against Saddam Hussein and Iraq. Tonight, our thoughts first of all go to them and their families.
Now a state of war exists. It demonstrates the full extent of our failure as politicians. The world has gone mad. We should not share Saddam Hussein's folly. One does not fight madness with madness.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, we agree that Saddam Hussein must be stopped. The new world order under which we thought we could thrive is being jeopardized by a tragic war. This is our first test since the last world war and we have failed miserably.

When I say "us", I do not just mean anyone in this House or any particular world leader, but as a world community. I think we can all agree that this is a failure.
It has been said that sometimes the first casualty of war is the truth. I have to say this with honesty, and perhaps others may share this feeling.
It is a feeling of betrayal for those of us who had hoped that economic sanctions would be given a chance, that there would be a true commitment by all world leaders, that all diplomatic efforts would be tried, and that war would be considered only as the last resort after all of these measures had been exhausted.
I have said it in other debates, Mr. Speaker, so I will not repeat it here, but we do not, as a party, agree that all those efforts were exhausted before this measure was taken-but, there is a war.
Today, in fact, our party unanimously supported an amendment to say that we should not participate in an offensive action against Iraq and we maintain that position.
I still believe that rather than saying Canadians should step aside, we should see what role we can really play-a role that would leave open the options not to not participate, but to participate in a meaningful way. Canada is a compassionate nation. We should exercise that compassion through our humanitarian work, through the kind of work that we see as being most useful to further the peace effort.
It is not a question of abdicating responsibility. It is a question of taking that responsibility in the most useful way possible, in the way that would lead to peace.
Hear, hear.

I share the comments of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition that we support our troops who are there. Of course we do. Of course our hearts are with those troops. Of course we feel that they are in danger and that we want to see the best for them. We want them to return home.
We hope the predictions that have been made about a long war will not be true. We would be quite happy to be proven wrong in this event.
The question is: how best do we support those troops? I would have to say, that in my view, the party's view, we support those troops by making sure that they are employed in actions that will truly show that Canada, as a compassionate nation, is prepared to participate, not within the theatre of war, but rather in a compassionate and humanitarian role for both civilians and non-civilians.
That is not non-participation, just as participating in economic sanctions was not non-participation. Let us be realistic that that view will not prevail. But I want to state clearly that that is our view.
Hear, hear.

I wish to speak directly to those men and women, those young people whose lives are so directly affected by this from coast to coast to coast. I speak to those people who have spoken out about their

concerns of a war, about Canada entering into a war and I say that you have not been defeated in your views tonight. I am sure that everyone in this House will work to bring about as quick a peace as is possible. But you must continue to express your views as all Canadians must, to give politicians the directions that we too need to reflect the best interest of Canada.
I say to these groups and individuals: we are with you. The New Democratic Party will continue to speak out against the madness of war.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, the choices have been made. They are not our choices. We will, each of us, live with the results of those choices. Each of us have taken, in our view, the most responsible position. We do not accuse those who disagree with us and we refuse to engage in debates about who has the greatest degree of morality.
Hear, hear.

Our disagreement is with the government's position. It is most assuredly not with the Canadian forces. We will be judged by history, but I want to assure Canadians and to assure this House that we will remain committed to a new world order, a genuinely new world order, and a new vision of a world in which war is no longer contemplated, a world of peace.
On the eve of war this may sound naive. This does not mean that Canada in any way abdicates its responsibility, but rather that Canada and the New Democratic Party will work for peace and international peace, to take our responsibilities seriously. We will not abandon the Canadian men and women in the Middle East. We will not engage in debates that are simply about who is right, but we will pursue that international vision based on a new world order, a new way to do things. We are committed to that.
In conclusion, I would simply like to say that I think everyone in Canada tonight is aware of the difficulty of this evening for everyone who must make decisions and those in particular who must bear the responsibility of our decisions. I say that our hearts are with them, our hearts are with their families. We, too, will work with the
Government Orders
government, with the Opposition, with any country, with any group to search for peace as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I had begun my comments just before the House suspended and we are now, I assume, continuing debate. With your guidance, Mr. Speaker-
Mr. Speaker The hon. member for Ottawa Vanier on a point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. I apologize to the House but I do think that most of us feel this moment to be one of momentous importance for the world and for Canadians in general.
We do not want at this time to engage in partisan debate on the motion before the House. I think the situation is very serious and we would like to have time to gather our thoughts, to really get the facts, come back to the House in due course and debate this very important situation tomorrow.
This for us is a momentous moment and I would ask the government to please adjourn the House which would give us a chance to get our facts together.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand the feelings of the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, but I too would like to have an opportunity this evening to respond to the speeches of the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party to say that, whether we like it or not, we are all at war regardless of our political affiliations. Our differences and nuances are theoretical and our alternatives are hypothetical.
In these times of great sadness I believe we all hope that the hostilities will end soon. We all hope that our sons and daughters, with the Iraqi civilians, will be able to avoid as many casualties as possible. We hope this war will not be for revenge but rather for the supremacy of international law. This evening we pray for all the men and women who are involved in this sad tragedy.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before I hear any further points of order-and I will certainly hear the hon. leader of the government-I remind hon. members that we are bound by the rules here.

January 16, 1991
Government Orders
This is an extraordinary day. Perhaps hon. members will want to deal with the situation in their own way. However, what I am dealing with now is a suggestion made by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier. The House leader of the Government wishes to have the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly the circumstances this evening have changed substantially, to put it mildly. The rules we had put in place and the special orders and so on may well have caused us to reconsider the procedures. There are of course not just the major parties but the Independents and people's desire to speak. I suggest to the House leader of the opposition Party and to the Leader of the New Democratic Party and other members that perhaps we can commence the continuation of the debate, use that time during the first speaker to discuss between ourselves and reach an accommodation that would allow us to meet.
Mr. Speaker I wonder if hon. members, keeping in mind what is taking place today, would give the House leader of the government a chance to respond fully.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I was suggesting this procedure as a result of not just the official parties but the Independents. Certainly, if you were to put the question and there was to be agreement, we would have no opposition.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can certainly say that on behalf of the New Democratic Party we think that to proceed now with the debate would be not only inappropriate, but almost bizarre. I would like to suggest that we seek unanimous consent of the House to terminate the debates for tonight. The House leaders can meet early in the morning to decide on the process for the next day, but I suspect that to proceed now would be totally inappropriate.
Mr. Speaker, I do agree with the suggestion of the House leader of the Liberal Party.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There seems to be agreement. I notice some of the other members are nodding in the direction of the Chair. It is so ordered.
Accordingly the House is adjourned until 11 a.m. tomorrow.

speechtext: The House adjourned at 10.47 p.m.
